drills.q: A stakeholder asks 'should we use ECS or Fargate for our new service?' How do you respond, and what's the actual question you should be answering instead?
drills.a: Point out this conflates two orthogonal axes — orchestrator (ECS vs EKS) and compute (EC2 vs Fargate). The real question is likely 'ECS or EKS' for orchestration, combined separately with 'EC2 or Fargate' for compute — answer both axes, not a false single choice.

drills.q: A platform team runs one EKS cluster per small internal tool (12 clusters, each with 1-3 services). Their AWS bill shows control-plane costs are a disproportionately large line item. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The flat ~$73/month EKS control-plane fee is being multiplied across 12 small clusters, even though the aggregate workload could plausibly fit on far fewer larger clusters where the fee would be negligible. Fix: consolidate onto fewer clusters using namespace-level isolation instead of one cluster per small service.

drills.q: A team runs a large, steady-state, highly predictable fleet entirely on Fargate and wants to cut costs without changing orchestrators. What's the first lever to pull, and why?
drills.a: Evaluate migrating the steady-state, predictable portion of the fleet to EC2-backed capacity (managed node groups, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler) — Fargate's real ~40-60% premium over equivalent EC2 compounds significantly at scale for predictable workloads, while its zero-node-management value is most justified for genuinely bursty/unpredictable portions, which should stay on Fargate.

drills.q: A pod on EKS fails to reach S3 with an access-denied error, even though `aws iam get-role-policy` confirms the referenced role has s3:GetObject. Where do you look next?
drills.a: The ServiceAccount-to-IAM-role association — check whether the IRSA annotation (or EKS Pod Identity association) actually links that ServiceAccount to that IAM role, and whether the pod spec references the correct ServiceAccount at all. A correct IAM policy is irrelevant if the federation linking pod identity to the role is missing or misconfigured.

drills.q: A team adds an EKS Fargate profile to an existing EC2-managed-node-group cluster to handle bursty batch jobs cheaply. A few weeks later they notice their node-level logging DaemonSet isn't capturing logs from the new batch job pods. Why, and what's the fix?
drills.a: DaemonSets cannot run on Fargate at all — there's no shared-node concept for the one-per-node pattern to attach to, so Fargate-profile pods are structurally invisible to any DaemonSet. Fix: add a sidecar container to the Fargate-profile pods for logging coverage instead, since the cluster now needs both patterns (DaemonSet for EC2 nodes, sidecars for Fargate pods).

drills.q: A new 5-person startup on AWS with no existing Kubernetes investment and no concrete multi-cloud plans is deciding between ECS and EKS. They mention they 'might need multi-cloud eventually.' What's the recommendation, and why?
drills.a: Recommend ECS + Fargate as the default — simpler operational model, no control-plane fee, smaller IAM learning curve. 'Might need it eventually' with no concrete funded plan is a weak signal; taking on EKS's real current operational complexity for a hypothetical future requirement is the same over-engineering mistake as premature module abstraction — migrate when the hypothetical becomes concrete.

drills.q: Nodes across a cluster start intermittently hitting ImagePullBackOff with rate-limit-flavored errors from Docker Hub, especially during scale-up events. What's the AWS-native production fix, and what changes in the manifests to use it?
drills.a: Configure an ECR pull-through cache rule for Docker Hub so pulls hit ECR (in-region, not subject to Docker Hub's rate limits) instead of the public registry directly. Image references in manifests must change to the ECR-proxied path (e.g. <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/docker-hub/library/redis:7) — it's not a transparent, zero-touch fix.

drills.q: An ECR repository has been accumulating images for two years with no storage management, and costs have crept up steadily. What's the standard fix, and what's the default behavior it's correcting?
drills.a: Attach a lifecycle policy (e.g. keep the last N tagged images per repository, expire untagged images after N days) — ECR retains every pushed image indefinitely by default with no automatic expiration, a slow, easy-to-overlook storage cost leak that compounds as CI continuously pushes new tagged and untagged images.
